The Christ would “proclaim light both to these people and to the Gentiles.” For Paul that was the hope of Israel itself, not a betrayal of it. (Acts 26:23)
The king said almost too. You wonder whether he ever got further. You wonder whether you will.

But he said, “I am not crazy, most excellent Festus, but boldly declare words of truth and reasonableness. For the king knows of these things, to whom also I speak freely. For I am persuaded that none of these things is hidden from him, for this has not been done in a corner. King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.”
but had certain questions against him about their own religion, and about one Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive.

But arise, and stand on your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose: to appoint you a servant and a witness both of the things which you have seen and of the things which I will reveal to you; delivering you from the people and from the Gentiles, to whom I send you, to open their eyes, that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive remission of sins and an inheritance among those who are sanctified by faith in me.’
Now when some days had passed, King Agrippa and Bernice arrived at Caesarea, and greeted Festus.
Agrippa said to Paul, “With a little persuasion are you trying to make me a Christian?”

Having therefore obtained the help that is from God, I stand to this day testifying both to small and great, saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would happen, how the Christ must suffer, and how, by the resurrection of the dead, he would be first to proclaim light both to these people and to the Gentiles.”
Paul said, “I pray to God, that whether with little or with much, not only you, but also all that hear me today, might become such as I am, except for these bonds.”

So on the next day, when Agrippa and Bernice had come with great pomp, and they had entered into the place of hearing with the commanding officers and principal men of the city, at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in.

The king rose up with the governor and Bernice, and those who sat with them. When they had withdrawn, they spoke to one another, saying, “This man does nothing worthy of death or of bonds.” Agrippa said to Festus, “This man might have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.”
Agrippa said to Paul, “You may speak for yourself.” Then Paul stretched out his hand, and made his defense.

“I think myself happy, King Agrippa, that I am to make my defense before you today concerning all the things that I am accused by the Jews, especially because you are expert in all customs and questions which are among the Jews. Therefore I beg you to hear me patiently.

“Therefore, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision, but declared first to them of Damascus, at Jerusalem, and throughout all the country of Judea, and also to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, doing works worthy of repentance. For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me.

“Whereupon as I traveled to Damascus with the authority and commission from the chief priests, at noon, O king, I saw on the way a light from the sky, brighter than the sun, shining around me and those who traveled with me. When we had all fallen to the earth, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’ “I said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ “He said, ‘I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.

“Indeed, all the Jews know my way of life from my youth up, which was from the beginning among my own nation and at Jerusalem; having known me from the first, if they are willing to testify, that after the strictest sect of our religion I lived a Pharisee. Now I stand here to be judged for the hope of the promise made by God to our fathers, which our twelve tribes, earnestly serving night and day, hope to attain. Concerning this hope I am accused by the Jews, King Agrippa! Why is it judged incredible with you if God does raise the dead?
Agrippa said to Festus, “I also would like to hear the man myself.” “Tomorrow,” he said, “you shall hear him.”

Of whom I have no certain thing to write to my lord. Therefore I have brought him out before you, and especially before you, King Agrippa, that, after examination, I may have something to write. For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to also specify the charges against him.”
As he thus made his defense, Festus said with a loud voice, “Paul, you are crazy! Your great learning is driving you insane!”

“I myself most certainly thought that I ought to do many things contrary to the name of Jesus of Nazareth. I also did this in Jerusalem. I both shut up many of the saints in prisons, having received authority from the chief priests; and when they were put to death I gave my vote against them. Punishing them often in all the synagogues, I tried to make them blaspheme. Being exceedingly enraged against them, I persecuted them even to foreign cities.
“Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.”
“He who hears, let him say, ‘Come!’” She stops, and waits for you. Your own scroll lies open on your knees, with room for one more line.

Patmos: bare rock, salt wind, and an old man writing. He was a fisherman’s son from Galilee. He stood at the cross. He ran to the tomb. He has outlived them all, and he is still writing down what he sees.
She writes it for you, in a young, clear hand, under all the years of yours. Then she reads the end.

It is nearly dawn in Ephesus. The others have gone home. The girl is still reading to you, and there is only a little of the scroll left in her right hand.
You began as someone sent to watch a carpenter from Nazareth, to see whether there was anything in it. You have told what you saw. The scroll is hers now, and whoever she reads it to.
“I was there. It is true.”

He who sits on the throne said, “Behold, I am making all things new.” He said, “Write, for these words of God are faithful and true.” He said to me, “It is done! I am the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End. I will give freely to him who is thirsty from the spring of the water of life. He who overcomes, I will give him these things. I will be his God, and he will be my son.

He showed me a river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb, in the middle of its street. On this side of the river and on that was the tree of life, bearing twelve kinds of fruits, yielding its fruit every month. The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.
He who testifies these things says, “Yes, I come quickly.” Amen! Yes, come, Lord Jesus. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with all the saints. Amen.

There will be no curse any more. The throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants serve him. They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. There will be no night, and they need no lamp light; for the Lord God will illuminate them. They will reign forever and ever.

I saw no temple in it, for the Lord God, the Almighty, and the Lamb, are its temple. The city has no need for the sun, neither of the moon, to shine, for the very glory of God illuminated it, and its lamp is the Lamb. The nations will walk in its light. The kings of the earth bring the glory and honor of the nations into it. Its gates will in no way be shut by day (for there will be no night there),

I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth have passed away, and the sea is no more. I saw the holy city, New Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, made ready like a bride adorned for her husband.

I heard a loud voice out of heaven saying, “Behold, God’s dwelling is with people, and he will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. He will wipe away from them every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more; neither will there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain, any more. The first things have passed away.”

I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify these things to you for the assemblies. I am the root and the offspring of David; the Bright and Morning Star.” The Spirit and the bride say, “Come!” He who hears, let him say, “Come!” He who is thirsty, let him come. He who desires, let him take the water of life freely.

A Greek believer, a dealer in dyed wool, invites Barnabas and you to supper. There is bread, and olives, and a dish of meat from the market. No one at this table knows where the meat was bought, or whether it was ever offered on an altar.
Barnabas is already eating. Your host passes you the dish.

“If God shows no favoritism, who else have I been calling unclean?” (Acts 10:28, 34)

The Greeks of Antioch, who believed and turned to the Lord. (Acts 11:20–21)
I ate at a Greek believer’s table, whatever was set before me.
Eat whatever is set before you.
I ate bread and olives at a Greek believer’s table.
Antioch on the Orontes: capital of Syria, one of the three great cities of the empire, with temples to the gods of Greece and Rome and a large Jewish quarter.
He nods, a little hurt, and lets you go. Barnabas watches you leave and says nothing.
Your host laughs and fills your cup. You think of a sheet let down from heaven, and of a voice that said three times not to call unclean what God has cleansed.
Thank them warmly, and eat later, alone.
You put in what you have, and watch Barnabas and Saul load the relief for Jerusalem: Greek money for Jewish believers, carried by a Levite and a Pharisee.

Barnabas brought Saul to Antioch, and the disciples were first called Christians there (Acts 11:26).
Write down the name they gave us.
Eat the bread and the olives, and nothing else.
Nobody minds. Your host keeps the bread coming. Later the believers will argue about these tables for years.
In Antioch, men from Cyprus and Cyrene preached the Lord Jesus to Greeks, and a great number believed (Acts 11:20–21).

Tarsus, chief city of Cilicia. Saul had been sent home here for his safety (Acts 9:30). By trade he was a tentmaker (18:3), working goat-hair cloth.
You came north with Barnabas, sent by the apostles to see whether the news from Antioch was true. It is.
I thanked my Greek host and ate later, alone.

Now in these days, prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. One of them named Agabus stood up, and indicated by the Spirit that there should be a great famine all over the world, which also happened in the days of Claudius.
As any of the disciples had plenty, each determined to send relief to the brothers who lived in Judea; which they also did, sending it to the elders by the hands of Barnabas and Saul.

When he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. It happened, that for a whole year they were gathered together with the assembly, and taught many people. The disciples were first called Christians in Antioch.
They therefore who were scattered abroad by the oppression that arose about Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except to Jews only.

But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who, when they had come to Antioch, spoke to the Hellenists, preaching the Lord Jesus. The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number believed and turned to the Lord.

The report concerning them came to the ears of the assembly which was in Jerusalem. They sent out Barnabas to go as far as Antioch, who, when he had come, and had seen the grace of God, was glad. He exhorted them all, that with purpose of heart they should remain near to the Lord. For he was a good man, and full of the Holy Spirit and of faith, and many people were added to the Lord.
Barnabas went out to Tarsus to look for Saul.
To quiet the rumors that he taught Jews to abandon the Law, the elders asked Paul to pay for the offerings of four men completing a vow, and to join them in the Temple (21:21–25).
Write it down. You are home, and he is in chains.
Stay at the foot of the stairs and listen.
Push toward the barracks gate to stay close to him.
You saw Trophimus yesterday, in the lower city. He never came near the Temple. You open your mouth to say so, and no one could hear you if you shouted.
You come back with James at a run in time to hear him tell the Damascus road. You were there for the beginning of that story. You never thought you would hear him tell it here.
He tells them the Damascus road: the light at noon, the voice, the blindness, Ananias. You were there for the beginning of that story. You never thought you would hear him tell it here.
Caesarea, by the sea: the house of Philip, who once ran beside a chariot on the desert road. He is grey now. His four daughters pour the wine.
Run to tell James and the elders.
About to be scourged, Paul asked, “Is it lawful for you to scourge a man who is a Roman, and not found guilty?” (Acts 22:25).
“Away with him!” The crowd cried the same thing outside Pilate’s gate, the morning they crucified Jesus. Where do you go?
On the stairs of the Antonia, Paul told the crowd his story in their own language. They listened until he spoke of being sent to the Gentiles (Acts 22:21–22).
You are home. You have not seen these walls in years. The city smells the same: smoke, sheep, the sea wind that never quite reaches it.
The four of them prophesy, Luke says, as easily as other girls sing. The youngest asks you about Jerusalem, and about the women who went to the tomb.

When the blood of Stephen, your witness, was shed, I also was standing by, and consenting to his death, and guarding the cloaks of those who killed him.’ “He said to me, ‘Depart, for I will send you out far from here to the Gentiles.’”
When he came to the stairs, it happened that he was carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd; for the multitude of the people followed after, crying out, “Away with him!”

Then Paul answered, “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.” When he would not be persuaded, we ceased, saying, “The Lord’s will be done.”
When we heard these things, both we and they of that place begged him not to go up to Jerusalem.

They listened to him until he said that; then they lifted up their voice, and said, “Rid the earth of this fellow, for he isn’t fit to live!” As they cried out, and threw off their cloaks, and threw dust into the air, the commanding officer commanded him to be brought into the barracks, ordering him to be examined by scourging, that he might know for what crime they shouted against him like that.

On the next day, we, who were Paul’s companions, departed, and came to Caesarea. We entered into the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him. Now this man had four virgin daughters who prophesied.

“Brothers and fathers, listen to the defense which I now make to you.” When they heard that he spoke to them in the Hebrew language, they were even more quiet. He said, “I am indeed a Jew, born in Tarsus of Cilicia, but brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, instructed according to the strict manner of the law of our fathers, being zealous for God, even as you all are this day. I persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering into prisons both men and women.

When we had come to Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly. The day following, Paul went in with us to James; and all the elders were present. When he had greeted them, he reported one by one the things which God had worked among the Gentiles through his ministry. They, when they heard it, glorified God. They said to him, “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews of those who have believed, and they are all zealous for the law.
As we stayed there some days, a certain prophet named Agabus came down from Judea.

Coming to us, and taking Paul’s belt, he bound his own feet and hands, and said, “Thus says the Holy Spirit: ‘So will the Jews at Jerusalem bind the man who owns this belt, and will deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles.’”

As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he asked the commanding officer, “May I speak to you?” He said, “Do you know Greek? Aren’t you then the Egyptian, who before these days stirred up to sedition and led out into the wilderness the four thousand men of the Assassins?” But Paul said, “I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city. I beg you, allow me to speak to the people.”

Immediately he took soldiers and centurions, and ran down to them. They, when they saw the chief captain and the soldiers, stopped beating Paul. Then the commanding officer came near, arrested him, commanded him to be bound with two chains, and inquired who he was and what he had done. Some shouted one thing, and some another, among the crowd. When he couldn’t find out the truth because of the noise, he commanded him to be brought into the barracks.

When they had tied him up with thongs, Paul asked the centurion who stood by, “Is it lawful for you to scourge a man who is a Roman, and not found guilty?” When the centurion heard it, he went to the commanding officer and told him, “Watch what you are about to do, for this man is a Roman!” The commanding officer came and asked him, “Tell me, are you a Roman?” He said, “Yes.” The commanding officer answered, “I bought my citizenship for a great price.” Paul said, “But I was born a Roman.” Immediately those who were about to examine him departed from him, and the commanding officer also was afraid when he realized that he was a Roman, because he had bound him.

He said, ‘The God of our fathers has appointed you to know his will, and to see the Righteous One, and to hear a voice from his mouth. For you will be a witness for him to all men of what you have seen and heard.

All the city was moved, and the people ran together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple. Immediately the doors were shut. As they were trying to kill him, news came up to the commanding officer of the regiment that all Jerusalem was in an uproar.

Then Paul took the men, and the next day, purified himself and went with them into the temple, declaring the fulfillment of the days of purification, until the offering was offered for every one of them.

When the seven days were almost completed, the Jews from Asia, when they saw him in the temple, stirred up all the multitude and laid hands on him, crying out, “Men of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches all men everywhere against the people, and the law, and this place. Moreover, he also brought Greeks into the temple, and has defiled this holy place!” For they had seen Trophimus, the Ephesian, with him in the city, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple.
Probably fifty thousand drachmas: roughly the wages of a laborer for a hundred and sixty years, turned to ash in an afternoon.
Two hours. You stop being able to hear the words. Only the beat of it remains, like a drum: Great is Artemis, great is Artemis, great is Artemis.
Stay hidden in the crowd and pray.
Afterward, at their table, Priscilla does most of the talking, and Aquila fills in what she leaves out. The great preacher from Alexandria listens like a student.
Go back to the gate and help hold Paul back.
At the gate Paul is still arguing to be let in when Gaius and Aristarchus walk out, alive. He holds them both for a long time.

Ephesus: the greatest city of Asia, a harbor full of ships, a temple that is one of the wonders of the world. Paul has gone on to Jerusalem and Antioch; Priscilla and Aquila have stayed, and so have you.
You find that you have been praying the same words for two hours, under the shouting. You do not remember starting.
For two hours the theater at Ephesus shouted “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” until the town clerk dismissed the assembly (Acts 19:28–41).
Push toward Gaius and Aristarchus.
Write it down while the city is quiet again.
Thousands are on their feet, shouting. Gaius and Aristarchus have been dragged into the middle. Paul is at the gate, trying to get in.

Afterward, at their table, Priscilla does most of the talking. The great preacher from Alexandria listens like a student. You have never seen a woman teach a man like that, so gently that he thanks her.
At Ephesus those who had practiced magic burned their books in the sight of all, worth fifty thousand pieces of silver (Acts 19:19).
The story goes around the city in a day. People who would never come to the school of Tyrannus repeat it in the market: the name of Jesus is not a charm to be borrowed.
Priscilla and Aquila took Apollos aside and explained the way of God to him more accurately (Acts 18:26).
You walk out of the theater with your arms around two shaking Macedonians, and nobody stops you.

He entered into the synagogue, and spoke boldly for a period of three months, reasoning and persuading about the things concerning the Kingdom of God. But when some were hardened and disobedient, speaking evil of the Way before the multitude, he departed from them, and separated the disciples, reasoning daily in the school of Tyrannus. This continued for two years, so that all those who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus, both Jews and Greeks.

Now a certain Jew named Apollos, an Alexandrian by race, an eloquent man, came to Ephesus. He was mighty in the Scriptures. This man had been instructed in the way of the Lord; and being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, although he knew only the baptism of John.

When the town clerk had quieted the multitude, he said, “You men of Ephesus, what man is there who doesn’t know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great goddess Artemis, and of the image which fell down from Zeus? Seeing then that these things can’t be denied, you ought to be quiet, and to do nothing rash. For you have brought these men here, who are neither robbers of temples nor blasphemers of your goddess.

If therefore Demetrius and the craftsmen who are with him have a matter against anyone, the courts are open, and there are proconsuls. Let them press charges against one another. But if you seek anything about other matters, it will be settled in the regular assembly. For indeed we are in danger of being accused concerning this day’s riot, there being no cause. Concerning it, we wouldn’t be able to give an account of this commotion.” When he had thus spoken, he dismissed the assembly.

When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. When Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they spoke with other languages and prophesied. They were about twelve men in all.

When Paul wanted to enter in to the people, the disciples didn’t allow him. Certain also of the Asiarchs, being his friends, sent to him and begged him not to venture into the theater. Some therefore cried one thing, and some another, for the assembly was in confusion. Most of them didn’t know why they had come together.
He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. But when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately.

Many of those who practiced magical arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. They counted the price of them, and found it to be fifty thousand pieces of silver. So the word of the Lord was growing and becoming mighty.
Now after these things had ended, Paul determined in the spirit, when he had passed through Macedonia and Achaia, to go to Jerusalem, saying, “After I have been there, I must also see Rome.”
God worked special miracles by the hands of Paul, so that even handkerchiefs or aprons were carried away from his body to the sick, and the evil spirits went out.

They brought Alexander out of the multitude, the Jews putting him forward. Alexander beckoned with his hand, and would have made a defense to the people. But when they perceived that he was a Jew, all with one voice for a time of about two hours cried out, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”
Many also of those who had believed came, confessing, and declaring their deeds.
The whole city was filled with confusion, and they rushed with one accord into the theater, having seized Gaius and Aristarchus, men of Macedonia, Paul’s companions in travel.

It happened that, while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul, having passed through the upper country, came to Ephesus, and found certain disciples. He said to them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” They said to him, “No, we haven’t even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.” He said, “Into what then were you baptized?” They said, “Into John’s baptism.” Paul said, “John indeed baptized with the baptism of repentance, saying to the people that they should believe in the one who would come after him, that is, in Jesus.”

About that time there arose no small stir concerning the Way. For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no little business to the craftsmen, whom he gathered together, with the workmen of like occupation, and said, “Sirs, you know that by this business we have our wealth. You see and hear, that not at Ephesus alone, but almost throughout all Asia, this Paul has persuaded and turned away many people, saying that they are no gods, that are made with hands. Not only is there danger that this our trade come into disrepute, but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be counted as nothing, and her majesty destroyed, whom all Asia and the world worships.”

When he had determined to pass over into Achaia, the brothers encouraged him, and wrote to the disciples to receive him. When he had come, he greatly helped those who had believed through grace; for he powerfully refuted the Jews, publicly showing by the Scriptures that Jesus was the Christ.
When they heard this they were filled with anger, and cried out, saying, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”

But some of the itinerant Jews, exorcists, took on themselves to invoke over those who had the evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus, saying, “We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preaches.” There were seven sons of one Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, who did this. The evil spirit answered, “Jesus I know, and Paul I know, but who are you?” The man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them, and overpowered them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded. This became known to all, both Jews and Greeks, who lived at Ephesus. Fear fell on them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified.
Some mocked; a few believed, among them Dionysius of the Areopagus and a woman named Damaris (Acts 17:32–34).
Write it down in the shadow of the Acropolis.

At the edge of the agora Paul stops at a small altar and reads the inscription aloud, twice, as if he cannot quite believe it.

Most of the Areopagus goes home to dinner. Two people stay behind to ask Paul where he is lodging. It does not look like much. You write it down anyway.
Walk with Paul and read the inscriptions with him.
“He is not far from each one of us.” You remember a scribe in the Temple courts, and Jesus telling him he was not far from the Kingdom of God.
You keep your eyes on the paving stones, and still the city looks back at you from every side.
You watch them instead: a woman leaving a cake of incense at a shrine, an old man touching a statue’s worn foot for luck, a boy asking his father which god is which. They are looking for something.
Turn away, and keep your eyes on the paving stones.
Watch the people instead of the statues.

Paul is alone in Athens, waiting for Silas and Timothy. Everywhere you look there is a god: in marble on the corners, in bronze at the doors, painted on the walls, carved into the very hill above the city.

Now while Paul waited for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw the city full of idols. So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who met him.

Paul stood in the middle of the Areopagus, and said, “You men of Athens, I perceive that you are very religious in all things. For as I passed along, and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with this inscription: ‘TO AN UNKNOWN GOD.’ What therefore you worship in ignorance, this I announce to you.

The times of ignorance therefore God overlooked. But now he commands that all people everywhere should repent, because he has appointed a day in which he will judge the world in righteousness by the man whom he has ordained; of which he has given assurance to all men, in that he has raised him from the dead.”

Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also were conversing with him. Some said, “What does this babbler want to say?” Others said, “He seems to be advocating foreign deities,” because he preached Jesus and the resurrection. They took hold of him, and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, “May we know what this new teaching is, which is spoken by you? For you bring certain strange things to our ears. We want to know therefore what these things mean.” Now all the Athenians and the strangers living there spent their time in nothing else, but either to tell or to hear some new thing.
But certain men joined with him, and believed, among whom also was Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them.

that they should seek the Lord, if perhaps they might reach out for him and find him, though he is not far from each one of us. ‘For in him we live, and move, and have our being.’ As some of your own poets have said, ‘For we are also his offspring.’ Being then the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Divine Nature is like gold, or silver, or stone, engraved by art and design of man.

The God who made the world and all things in it, he, being Lord of heaven and earth, doesn’t dwell in temples made with hands, neither is he served by men’s hands, as though he needed anything, seeing he himself gives to all life and breath, and all things. He made from one blood every nation of men to dwell on all the surface of the earth, having determined appointed seasons, and the boundaries of their dwellings,
Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked; but others said, “We want to hear you again concerning this.” Thus Paul went out from among them.
The Bereans received the word with readiness, examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so (Acts 17:11).
You stand beside Jason in the doorway. The torchlight is in your eyes. Someone spits.
Fists on the door. Torches in the street. Jason looks at you.
The Psalm: “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit by my right hand.’”
You run through the alleys knocking on doors you were shown only three days ago.
From Philippi you walk west for days along the Via Egnatia, the great paved road of Macedonia, still stiff from the night in Philippi.
You find the place in Isaiah that the Ethiopian was reading on the desert road, and read it aloud. The room is quiet for a long time.
Slip out the back to warn the brothers.
You pull a hanging behind them and stand in front of it, as if you were only a guest who had been asleep.

lines.speaker: The elder
lines.text: Tomorrow we will read it again. And the day after.
The Psalm: “You will not leave my soul in Hades.”
Three scrolls lie open on the table. Which do you unroll first?
Isaiah: “He was led as a sheep to the slaughter.”
Write it down. Then check what you wrote against the Scriptures.

lines.speaker: An elder of the synagogue
lines.text: You are from Jerusalem, and you can read. Good. He says the Christ had to suffer and rise. Show us where.
You go down to the coast with the brothers who are taking Paul to Athens. Silas and Timothy stay behind. So, for now, does the old man with his finger on the page.
In Thessalonica the mob cried that we had turned the world upside down, saying there is another king, Jesus (Acts 17:6–7).
Stand at the door with Jason and face the crowd.
You find the psalm Peter quoted at Pentecost, and the old man reads it again with his finger under every word.
You find the psalm that Jesus himself asked the scribes about in the Temple courts, and tell them what he asked.
Hide Paul and Silas in the back of the house.

Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a Jewish synagogue. Paul, as was his custom, went in to them, and for three Sabbath days reasoned with them from the Scriptures, explaining and demonstrating that the Christ had to suffer and rise again from the dead, and saying, “This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ.”

But when the Jews of Thessalonica had knowledge that the word of God was proclaimed by Paul at Beroea also, they came there likewise, agitating the multitudes. Then the brothers immediately sent out Paul to go as far as to the sea, and Silas and Timothy still stayed there. But those who escorted Paul brought him as far as Athens. Receiving a commandment to Silas and Timothy that they should come to him very quickly, they departed.
Some of them were persuaded, and joined Paul and Silas, of the devout Greeks a great multitude, and not a few of the chief women.
Many of them therefore believed; also of the prominent Greek women, and not a few men.
The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Beroea. When they arrived, they went into the Jewish synagogue.
But the unpersuaded Jews took along some wicked men from the marketplace, and gathering a crowd, set the city in an uproar. Assaulting the house of Jason, they sought to bring them out to the people.
Now these were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of the mind, examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so.

When they didn’t find them, they dragged Jason and certain brothers before the rulers of the city, crying, “These who have turned the world upside down have come here also, whom Jason has received. These all act contrary to the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus!” The multitude and the rulers of the city were troubled when they heard these things. When they had taken security from Jason and the rest, they let them go.
Touching the dead will make you unclean for seven days. You will not eat the Passover with your family (Numbers 9:6). What do you do?
Watch with the women from Galilee.
Carry the spice jars only.
A stone was rolled against the door of the tomb, and the women saw where he was laid (Mark 15:46–47).
I carried the spices for Nicodemus.
You knew him before, didn’t you?
Nicodemus came to him by night, and was told, “You must be born anew” (John 3:7).
What do you ask your uncle?
I held back and watched from the garden wall.
Write your report by lamplight, when the Sabbath is over.
I watched with the women from Galilee.

Write your letter by lamplight, when the Sabbath is over.
Carry the spices only.

Did you ever speak up for him in the council?

Help wind the linen and the spices.

lines.text: “So must the Son of Man be lifted up.” I did not understand it then. Tonight I think I do.

Hold back and watch.

lines.speaker: Nicodemus
lines.text: They laughed at me. I let them. I should have said more, and sooner.
Nicodemus asked the council to give him a hearing first, and they mocked him for it (John 7:50–52).

lines.speaker: Nicodemus
lines.text: You came. Good. Joseph has the governor’s permission, and we have until sunset. Joseph’s servants will carry him. I need your hands for the linen and the spices.
What else do you ask?
Help carry him.

lines.speaker: Nicodemus
lines.text: I went to him at night, so that no one would see me. I am an old man, and I asked him how a man could be born again.
What do you ask your teacher?
Helping to wrap the body will make you unclean for seven days. You will not eat the Passover with your family (Numbers 9:6). What do you do?
Joseph and Nicodemus wrapped his body with the spices in linen and laid it in a new tomb in a garden (John 19:40–41).
Pilate marveled if he were already dead; and summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he had been dead long. When he found out from the centurion, he granted the body to Joseph.

After these things, Joseph of Arimathaea, being a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, asked of Pilate that he might take away Jesus’ body. Pilate gave him permission. He came therefore and took away his body. Nicodemus, who at first came to Jesus by night, also came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds.

He bought a linen cloth, and taking him down, wound him in the linen cloth, and laid him in a tomb which had been cut out of a rock. He rolled a stone against the door of the tomb. Mary Magdalene and Mary, the mother of Joses, saw where he was laid.

Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. The same came to him by night, and said to him, “Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do, unless God is with him.”

Jesus answered, “Most certainly I tell you, unless one is born of water and spirit, he can’t enter into the Kingdom of God! That which is born of the flesh is flesh. That which is born of the Spirit is spirit. Don’t marvel that I said to you, ‘You must be born anew.’ The wind blows where it wants to, and you hear its sound, but don’t know where it comes from and where it is going. So is everyone who is born of the Spirit.”

Jesus answered him, “Most certainly, I tell you, unless one is born anew, he can’t see the Kingdom of God.” Nicodemus said to him, “How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb, and be born?”

So they took Jesus’ body, and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as the custom of the Jews is to bury. Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden. In the garden was a new tomb in which no man had ever yet been laid. Then because of the Jews’ Preparation Day (for the tomb was near at hand) they laid Jesus there.

Nicodemus answered him, “How can these things be?” Jesus answered him, “Are you the teacher of Israel, and don’t understand these things? Most certainly I tell you, we speak that which we know, and testify of that which we have seen, and you don’t receive our witness. If I told you earthly things and you don’t believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things? No one has ascended into heaven, but he who descended out of heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven.

Nicodemus (he who came to him by night, being one of them) said to them, “Does our law judge a man, unless it first hears from him personally and knows what he does?” They answered him, “Are you also from Galilee? Search, and see that no prophet has arisen out of Galilee.”

As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. For God so loved the world, that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.

The officers therefore came to the chief priests and Pharisees, and they said to them, “Why didn’t you bring him?” The officers answered, “No man ever spoke like this man!” The Pharisees therefore answered them, “You aren’t also led astray, are you? Have any of the rulers believed in him, or of the Pharisees? But this multitude that doesn’t know the law is accursed.”

When evening had now come, because it was the Preparation Day, that is, the day before the Sabbath, Joseph of Arimathaea, a prominent council member who also himself was looking for the Kingdom of God, came. He boldly went in to Pilate, and asked for Jesus’ body.
A fisherman said half the village had waited at one door since dawn.
Go down to the shore by the boat and write your report.
The paralyzed man got up, took his mat, and walked out in front of everyone (Mark 2:12).
Walk to the shore
He answered what the scribes were thinking before anyone spoke (Mark 2:8).
Outside, the street is full of people talking at once.

lines.speaker: A fisherman mending nets
lines.text: Looking for Jesus of Nazareth? Follow the noise. Half the village has been at that door since dawn.
“Why does this man speak blasphemies like that? Who can forgive sins but God alone?”
He is speaking the word to them. Look around the room and tap anything worth noting in your scroll.

lines.speaker: The woman at the quern
lines.text: Did you see him? He walked past me carrying his own mat!
Inside, the air is close and warm. Bodies press against the walls. As a teacher of the Law, you are waved to a place on the floor near the front, among the other scribes.
Go down to the shore by the boat and write your letter.
Words like these belong to God alone. What rises in your heart?
Find the house where Jesus is staying. Tap the street to walk; tap people to talk.

Inside, the air is close and warm. Bodies press against the walls. You squeeze in by the door with the women of the household. From here you can see the teacher, and the row of scribes from Jerusalem sitting on the floor in front of him.
He told the paralyzed man his sins were forgiven (Mark 2:5).
Say nothing. Watch what happens next.

lines.speaker: One of the four friends
lines.text: We couldn’t get him through the door. So we went up.
A question is now open in your scroll
She is describing an earlier day in Capernaum, recorded in Mark 1:29–31.
Capernaum, on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee. Houses of black basalt crowd around shared courtyards. Their flat roofs are beams and branches packed with earth.

lines.speaker: A woman grinding grain
lines.text: You’ve come about him? He healed Simon’s wife’s mother, here in this village. The fever left her, and she got up and served them.
People are praising God on every side. You came to write down what you saw. You saw this.
No one has spoken aloud. Yet he turns from the man on the mat and looks along the row of scribes. At you.
Added to your scroll
Go to the house

lines.speaker: Someone in the crowd
lines.text: You won’t get in that way, friend. Oh — a teacher of the Law. Make way, make way!
Villagers say he healed Simon’s mother-in-law of a fever here (Mark 1:29–31).
Something scrapes overhead. Dust sifts down between the beams. One by one, faces turn upward.
No one has spoken aloud. Yet he turns from the man on the mat, looks along the row of scribes, and then past them to the doorway. At you.
Only God forgives sins. So who does he think he is?

lines.speaker: Someone in the crowd
lines.text: You won’t get in that way, daughter. Squeeze in by the door with the women of the house; you will see from there.
Keep listening

When he entered again into Capernaum after some days, it was heard that he was in the house. Immediately many were gathered together, so that there was no more room, not even around the door; and he spoke the word to them.
He arose, and immediately took up the mat, and went out in front of them all; so that they were all amazed, and glorified God, saying, “We never saw anything like this!”

It happened on one of those days, that he was teaching; and there were Pharisees and teachers of the law sitting by, who had come out of every village of Galilee, Judea, and Jerusalem. The power of the Lord was with him to heal them.
But there were some of the scribes sitting there, and reasoning in their hearts, “Why does this man speak blasphemies like that? Who can forgive sins but God alone?”

Four people came, carrying a paralytic to him. When they could not come near to him for the crowd, they removed the roof where he was. When they had broken it up, they let down the mat that the paralytic was lying on.

Immediately Jesus, perceiving in his spirit that they so reasoned within themselves, said to them, “Why do you reason these things in your hearts? Which is easier, to tell the paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven;’ or to say, ‘Arise, and take up your bed, and walk?’
But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—he said to the paralytic— “I tell you, arise, take up your mat, and go to your house.”
Jesus, seeing their faith, said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven you.”
Pray for him: the man who just accused you.
In the night the Lord told Paul, “Don’t be afraid… for I am with you… for I have many people in this city” (Acts 18:9–10).
By the time you reach him the crowd has had its fill and drifted away. You help him sit up. He looks at you, a believer from Jerusalem, and does not understand why you came.
You wake in the night. Paul is on his knees by the window, and the room is full of a light that does not come from the lamp.
When the crowd drifts away he is sitting alone in the dust below the judgment seat. You cannot stop thinking about it.
You pray for him by name, and are surprised to find that you mean it.
Years later, Paul’s first letter to this city was sent from Paul “and our brother Sosthenes” (1 Corinthians 1:1). It may be the same man.
After Athens, Paul is quiet. He came to Corinth, he will later write, “in weakness, in fear, and in much trembling.” For now he cuts goat-hair cloth and says little.
They are beating the ruler of the synagogue in front of the judgment seat, and the proconsul is looking the other way.
Push through the crowd toward Sosthenes.
The proconsul Gallio refused to judge “questions about words and names and your own law” and drove the accusers from the judgment seat (Acts 18:14–16).
The ruler of the synagogue walks next door to the house where Paul has gone. Half the room watches him go.
You stand on the quay at Cenchreae and watch the ship go: Paul with his head newly shaved, and Priscilla and Aquila, who left Rome with nothing and are leaving Corinth with a church.
Write it down on the quay at Cenchreae.
Stand back, sick at heart.
Aquila shows you how to wax the thread and set the awl. Your stitches are crooked. He unpicks them without a word and hands the work back to you.

Priscilla shows you how to wax the thread and set the awl. She talks while she sews, about Rome, about the night they had to leave, about the Scriptures, which she knows better than most men you have met.
Then all the Greeks laid hold on Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him before the judgment seat. Gallio didn’t care about any of these things.
He lived there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.
He drove them from the judgment seat.

He reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, and persuaded Jews and Greeks. But when Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul was compelled by the Spirit, testifying to the Jews that Jesus was the Christ.
When they opposed him and blasphemed, he shook out his clothing and said to them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am clean. From now on, I will go to the Gentiles!”

After these things Paul departed from Athens, and came to Corinth. He found a certain Jew named Aquila, a man of Pontus by race, who had recently come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to depart from Rome. He came to them, and because he practiced the same trade, he lived with them and worked, for by trade they were tent makers.
Paul, having stayed after this many more days, took his leave of the brothers, and sailed from there for Syria, together with Priscilla and Aquila. He shaved his head in Cenchreae, for he had a vow.

But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, “If indeed it were a matter of wrong or of wicked crime, you Jews, it would be reasonable that I should bear with you; but if they are questions about words and names and your own law, look to it yourselves. For I don’t want to be a judge of these matters.”
The Lord said to Paul in the night by a vision, “Don’t be afraid, but speak and don’t be silent; for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many people in this city.”
Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord with all his house. Many of the Corinthians, when they heard, believed and were baptized.
He departed there, and went into the house of a certain man named Justus, one who worshiped God, whose house was next door to the synagogue.
But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews with one accord rose up against Paul and brought him before the judgment seat, saying, “This man persuades men to worship God contrary to the law.”
Wait in the doorway.
Peter stops at the door for a moment. So do you.
You are inside before you have decided to be.
The brothers from Joppa stare. So do you. It is the same as Pentecost: the same gift, the same praise in other languages, on Romans.
Write down who God has made clean.
Meanwhile, about fifty kilometers up the coast in Caesarea, the most Roman city in the land.
Men sent by a Roman centurion came to the tanner’s gate, and Peter took them in as his guests (Acts 10:23).
You are the one who opens the gate. Two household servants and a soldier of Rome stand in the street of a Jewish house, asking for Peter by name.
Step over the threshold behind Peter.
Peter saw a sheet full of unclean animals, and heard, “What God has cleansed, you must not call unclean” (Acts 10:15).
Noon in the tanner’s house. You are helping Simon’s wife with the bread when Peter climbs the outside stairs to the roof to pray.
He tells them everything in order: the roof, the sheet, the men at the gate, the house in Caesarea.

“Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners?” (Mark 2:16)

God shows no favoritism. What God has cleansed, you must not call unclean. (Acts 10:15, 34)
While Peter was still speaking, the Holy Spirit fell on the Gentiles, and they were baptized in the name of Jesus Christ (Acts 10:44–48).
Go in first, so that he will not be the only one.
The doorway is painted red and gold. Beyond it the floor is a mosaic of a kind you have only heard described. You have never in your life crossed a Gentile’s threshold.

God raised him up the third day, and gave him to be revealed, not to all the people, but to witnesses who were chosen before by God, to us, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead. He charged us to preach to the people and to testify that this is he who is appointed by God as the Judge of the living and the dead. All the prophets testify about him, that through his name everyone who believes in him will receive remission of sins.”
A voice came to him, “Rise, Peter, kill and eat!”
When it happened that Peter entered, Cornelius met him, fell down at his feet, and worshiped him. But Peter raised him up, saying, “Stand up! I myself am also a man.”

Now the apostles and the brothers who were in Judea heard that the Gentiles had also received the word of God. When Peter had come up to Jerusalem, those who were of the circumcision contended with him, saying, “You went in to uncircumcised men, and ate with them!” But Peter began, and explained to them in order, saying,
So he called them in and lodged them. On the next day Peter arose and went out with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him.
But Peter said, “Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean.” A voice came to him again the second time, “What God has cleansed, you must not call unclean.”

that spoken word you yourselves know, which was proclaimed throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee, after the baptism which John preached; even Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power, who went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him. We are witnesses of everything he did both in the country of the Jews, and in Jerusalem; whom they also killed, hanging him on a tree.
When they heard these things, they held their peace, and glorified God, saying, “Then God has also granted to the Gentiles repentance to life!”

While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell on all those who heard the word. They of the circumcision who believed were amazed, as many as came with Peter, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was also poured out on the nations. For they heard them speaking in other languages and magnifying God. Then Peter answered,
He commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to stay some days.
While Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Behold, three men seek you. But arise, get down, and go with them, doubting nothing; for I have sent them.”

He saw heaven opened and a certain container descending to him, like a great sheet let down by four corners on the earth, in which were all kinds of four-footed animals of the earth, wild animals, reptiles, and birds of the sky.

Now while Peter was very perplexed in himself what the vision which he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon’s house, stood before the gate, and called and asked whether Simon, who was surnamed Peter, was lodging there.

At about the ninth hour of the day, he clearly saw in a vision an angel of God coming to him, and saying to him, “Cornelius!” He, fastening his eyes on him, and being frightened, said, “What is it, Lord?” He said to him, “Your prayers and your gifts to the needy have gone up for a memorial before God. Now send men to Joppa, and get Simon, who is surnamed Peter. He lodges with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the seaside.”

Peter opened his mouth and said, “Truly I perceive that God doesn’t show favoritism; but in every nation he who fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him. The word which he sent to the children of Israel, preaching good news of peace by Jesus Christ—he is Lord of all—

Now there was a certain man in Caesarea, Cornelius by name, a centurion of what was called the Italian Regiment, a devout man, and one who feared God with all his house, who gave gifts for the needy generously to the people, and always prayed to God.
“Can any man forbid the water, that these who have received the Holy Spirit as well as we should not be baptized?”

As he talked with him, he went in and found many gathered together. He said to them, “You yourselves know how it is an unlawful thing for a man who is a Jew to join himself or come to one of another nation, but God has shown me that I shouldn’t call any man unholy or unclean. Therefore also I came without complaint when I was sent for. I ask therefore, why did you send for me?”
On the next day they entered into Caesarea. Cornelius was waiting for them, having called together his relatives and his near friends.

Cornelius said, “Four days ago, I was fasting until this hour, and at the ninth hour, I prayed in my house, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing, and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer is heard, and your gifts to the needy are remembered in the sight of God. Send therefore to Joppa, and summon Simon, who is surnamed Peter. He lodges in the house of Simon a tanner, by the seaside. When he comes, he will speak to you.’ Therefore I sent to you at once, and it was good of you to come. Now therefore we are all here present in the sight of God to hear all things that have been commanded you by God.”

As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them, even as on us at the beginning. I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, ‘John indeed baptized in water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit.’ If then God gave to them the same gift as us, when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I, that I could withstand God?”

Now on the next day as they were on their journey, and got close to the city, Peter went up on the housetop to pray at about noon. He became hungry and desired to eat, but while they were preparing, he fell into a trance.

Peter went down to the men, and said, “Behold, I am he whom you seek. Why have you come?” They said, “Cornelius, a centurion, a righteous man and one who fears God, and well spoken of by all the nation of the Jews, was directed by a holy angel to invite you to his house, and to listen to what you say.”
This was done three times, and immediately the vessel was received up into heaven.

When the angel who spoke to him had departed, Cornelius called two of his household servants and a devout soldier of those who waited on him continually. Having explained everything to them, he sent them to Joppa.
You come down the stairs into the courtyard, your notes under your arm. The Galilean is still at the fire.
Below in the courtyard, Peter denied him three times and wept (Mark 14:66–72).
The council sits in a half circle in the lamplight. Your teacher Nicodemus stands at the end of a bench. He does not look at you.
False witnesses spoke against him, but their testimony did not agree (Mark 14:56, 59).
On the high priest, as you were trained.
On him.
A Galilean fisherman, one of his disciples, sat warming himself at the high priest’s fire.
You are a junior scribe; no one asks for your vote. Every hand around you goes up. In Capernaum you thought the same word in silence: blasphemy.
By the fire sits a big Galilean you have seen before, on the shore at Capernaum. He keeps his face to the flames.
Asked if he was the Christ, he answered, “I am” (Mark 14:62).
On the floor.
Past midnight, a servant of the high priest pounds on your door. The council is gathering at once, and every scribe who can take notes is wanted.
On the high priest, as a servant would.
He is already looking at you across the room, the way he looked to the doorway in Capernaum.
The room waits for his answer. Where are your eyes?
He is already looking at you, the way he looked along the row of scribes in Capernaum.
He goes out into the dark, weeping. For a moment you want to follow him.
The council condemned him for blasphemy (Mark 14:64).
You stand by the door with the servants of the house, holding your uncle’s writing case. The council sits in a half circle in the lamplight. Nicodemus does not look at you.
Dawn is coming. Write down what you saw this night.

Past midnight, a servant of the high priest pounds on your uncle’s door. The council is gathering at once. Nicodemus takes you with him to carry his writing case; you will wait with the servants of the house.
No one in this room would ask a woman by the door what she thinks. Every hand on the benches goes up. In Capernaum you heard the same word muttered by the scribes: blasphemy.

As Peter was in the courtyard below, one of the maids of the high priest came, and seeing Peter warming himself, she looked at him, and said, “You were also with the Nazarene, Jesus!” But he denied it, saying, “I neither know, nor understand what you are saying.” He went out on the porch, and the rooster crowed.
The high priest tore his clothes, and said, “What further need have we of witnesses? You have heard the blasphemy! What do you think?” They all condemned him to be worthy of death.

Some stood up, and gave false testimony against him, saying, “We heard him say, ‘I will destroy this temple that is made with hands, and in three days I will build another made without hands.’” Even so, their testimony did not agree.
But he began to curse, and to swear, “I don’t know this man of whom you speak!”
Jesus said, “I am. You will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of the sky.”

The maid saw him, and began again to tell those who stood by, “This is one of them.” But he again denied it. After a little while again those who stood by said to Peter, “You truly are one of them, for you are a Galilean, and your speech shows it.”

They led Jesus away to the high priest. All the chief priests, the elders, and the scribes came together with him. Peter had followed him from a distance, until he came into the court of the high priest. He was sitting with the officers, and warming himself in the light of the fire.

The high priest stood up in the midst, and asked Jesus, “Have you no answer? What is it which these testify against you?” But he stayed quiet, and answered nothing. Again the high priest asked him, “Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?”
The rooster crowed the second time. Peter remembered the word, how that Jesus said to him, “Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.” When he thought about that, he wept.
Some began to spit on him, and to cover his face, and to beat him with fists, and to tell him, “Prophesy!” The officers struck him with the palms of their hands.

Now the chief priests and the whole council sought witnesses against Jesus to put him to death, and found none. For many gave false testimony against him, and their testimony didn’t agree with each other.
They have reached the place. Where do you stand?
The centurion who stood facing him said, “Truly this man was the Son of God!” (Mark 15:39).
Two of the men laughing at the foot of the hill taught you the Law. What do you do?
Far off, with the women from Galilee.
I stood near the road where the crowd and my uncle’s friends stood.
Two of the men laughing at the foot of the hill have eaten at your uncle’s table. What do you do?
The veil hung before the Most Holy Place in the Temple, where only the high priest went, once a year.
Morning. The council has handed him to Pilate, and Pilate has handed him to the soldiers. You stand by the road outside the gate with the crowd.
Keep your eyes on him.
Turn your back on them.
I stood far off, with the women who had followed him from Galilee.
Over him was written the charge: “THE KING OF THE JEWS” (Mark 15:26).
I stood near the road where the crowd and my teachers stood.
Stay with the women until evening. Then write what you saw.

People drift back toward the gate. The women do not move. Neither do you.
Near the road, with the crowd and the scribes.
Say nothing.

When the sixth hour had come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour.

Some of those who stood by, when they heard it, said, “Behold, he is calling Elijah.” One ran, and filling a sponge full of vinegar, put it on a reed, and gave it to him to drink, saying, “Let him be. Let’s see whether Elijah comes to take him down.”

Likewise, also the chief priests mocking among themselves with the scribes said, “He saved others. He can’t save himself. Let the Christ, the King of Israel, now come down from the cross, that we may see and believe him.” Those who were crucified with him insulted him.

There were also women watching from afar, among whom were both Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the less and of Joses, and Salome; who, when he was in Galilee, followed him, and served him; and many other women who came up with him to Jerusalem.
At the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, “Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?” which is, being interpreted, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”
Jesus cried out with a loud voice, and gave up the spirit.

The soldiers led him away within the court, which is the Praetorium; and they called together the whole cohort. They clothed him with purple, and weaving a crown of thorns, they put it on him. They began to salute him, “Hail, King of the Jews!” They struck his head with a reed, and spat on him, and bowing their knees, did homage to him. When they had mocked him, they took the purple off of him, and put his own garments on him. They led him out to crucify him.
When the centurion, who stood by opposite him, saw that he cried out like this and breathed his last, he said, “Truly this man was the Son of God!”
The veil of the temple was torn in two from the top to the bottom.

They offered him wine mixed with myrrh to drink, but he didn’t take it. Crucifying him, they parted his garments among them, casting lots on them, what each should take. It was the third hour, and they crucified him.
They brought him to the place called Golgotha, which is, being interpreted, “The place of a skull.”
You hand him the scroll. He unrolls it and reads in silence for a long time, a year and more of things seen and heard, with the dates and the names of witnesses.
Paphos, the Roman capital of Cyprus, a hundred and fifty kilometers west across the island.
You have never been to sea. By the second hour you are sick over the rail, and Saul, who has sailed before, brings you water and does not laugh.
Toward evening a long blue island lifts out of the sea. Barnabas stands at the bow and says nothing at all.
Write it down. Begin with the name.

lines.speaker: Sergius Paulus
lines.text: My adviser says these are fables from Judea. You there, from Jerusalem. Were you there? Did you see any of it yourself?

You look at Paul, and Paul begins. You realize that he too is a witness: of the road to Damascus, and of the man he once hunted.
Let Paul answer for both of you.
A Levite from Cyprus, Simeon called Niger, “the Black,” a man from Cyrene, a man who grew up in Herod’s palace, and the Pharisee from Tarsus. You have never seen a council like this one.
Hand him your scroll and let him read.
The governor of Cyprus is looking at you.

Barnabas asks you to come as far as Cyprus with his cousin’s family, who are going home to Salamis. He has letters for his kin, and he would like a witness from Jerusalem along.
The church at Antioch fasted, prayed, laid hands on Barnabas and Saul, and sent them away (Acts 13:2–3).
At Paphos the proconsul Sergius Paulus believed, astonished at the teaching of the Lord (Acts 13:12).

Yes. In Paphos a Roman governor asked what I had seen, and I told him. (Acts 1:8; 4:20)
Tell him what you saw with your own eyes.

But Elymas the sorcerer (for so is his name by interpretation) withstood them, seeking to turn aside the proconsul from the faith.

When they had gone through the island to Paphos, they found a certain sorcerer, a false prophet, a Jew, whose name was Bar Jesus, who was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a man of understanding. This man summoned Barnabas and Saul, and sought to hear the word of God.
When they were at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the Jewish synagogues. They had also John as their attendant.

Now, behold, the hand of the Lord is on you, and you will be blind, not seeing the sun for a season!” Immediately a mist and darkness fell on him. He went around seeking someone to lead him by the hand.
As they served the Lord and fasted, the Holy Spirit said, “Separate Barnabas and Saul for me, for the work to which I have called them.”
Then, when they had fasted and prayed and laid their hands on them, they sent them away.
Then the proconsul, when he saw what was done, believed, being astonished at the teaching of the Lord.

Now in the assembly that was at Antioch there were some prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen the foster brother of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul.
Now Paul and his company set sail from Paphos, and came to Perga in Pamphylia. John departed from them and returned to Jerusalem.

But Saul, who is also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, fastened his eyes on him, and said, “Full of all deceit and all cunning, you son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, will you not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord?

“Who is the young man named Saul?” (Acts 7:58)

Saul of Tarsus, a Pharisee, who met the risen Jesus on the road and became his chosen vessel. (Acts 9:15)
An old disciple named Ananias and his wife take you in. Before supper he kneels to pray, and does not get up for a long time. Then he speaks aloud, to someone you cannot see.
On the road, a light from the sky; a voice: “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting” (Acts 9:3–5).
Tell him you are afraid too.
Pray for Saul before you go.
Saul sits down to eat. You have one question.
You pray for the man who kept the cloaks. It is the hardest prayer you have ever prayed. Somewhere across the city, he is praying too.
Years from now he will tell a crowd in Jerusalem what he told you tonight:
You traveled north for a week with a caravan of believers to warn the disciples in Damascus that Saul was coming with letters. You are too late, though not in the way you feared.
What happened on the road?
Saul has your name on his list. Ananias is looking at you.

Write it down. No one in Jerusalem will believe it.

lines.speaker: Ananias
lines.text: Good. So am I. Let us be afraid together, then, and go.

lines.speaker: Saul
lines.text: They tell me you were outside the gate when Stephen died. I was there too. I kept the cloaks. I thought I was serving God.
When Saul goes up to Jerusalem at last, the believers there will be afraid of him. It will take a Levite from Cyprus to vouch for him.
He has not eaten in three days. His eyes are open, and they see nothing.
Go with him without a word.

lines.speaker: Saul
lines.text: I know you. You were by the cloaks, watching me as I watched him. I thought I was serving God that day.

lines.speaker: Ananias
lines.text: He says Saul of Tarsus is praying on Straight Street, at the house of Judah. He says I am to lay my hands on him.
You walked north for a week to warn the believers in Damascus that Saul was coming with letters. You are too late, though not in the way you feared.
An old disciple named Ananias takes you in. Before supper he kneels to pray, and does not get up for a long time. Then he speaks aloud, to someone you cannot see.
You stood beside Saul when Stephen died. You know his face. Ananias is looking at you.
“The Way” is what the believers are called. Saul’s letters name you, too, though he does not know your face.

Ananias departed, and entered into the house. Laying his hands on him, he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord, who appeared to you on the road by which you came, has sent me, that you may receive your sight, and be filled with the Holy Spirit.”
He took food and was strengthened. Saul stayed several days with the disciples who were at Damascus.
As he traveled, it happened that he got close to Damascus, and suddenly a light from the sky shone around him.
Immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he received his sight. He arose and was baptized.

But Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest, and asked for letters from him to the synagogues of Damascus, that if he found any who were of the Way, whether men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.

But the Lord said to him, “Go your way, for he is my chosen vessel to bear my name before the nations and kings, and the children of Israel. For I will show him how many things he must suffer for my name’s sake.”
The men who traveled with him stood speechless, hearing the sound, but seeing no one.

When Saul had come to Jerusalem, he tried to join himself to the disciples; but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple. But Barnabas took him, and brought him to the apostles, and declared to them how he had seen the Lord in the way, and that he had spoken to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus.

He fell on the earth, and heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” He said, “Who are you, Lord?” The Lord said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. But rise up, and enter into the city, and you will be told what you must do.”

Immediately in the synagogues he proclaimed the Christ, that he is the Son of God. All who heard him were amazed, and said, “Isn’t this he who in Jerusalem made havoc of those who called on this name? And he had come here intending to bring them bound before the chief priests!” But Saul increased more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived at Damascus, proving that this is the Christ.
Saul arose from the ground, and when his eyes were opened, he saw no one. They led him by the hand, and brought him into Damascus. He was without sight for three days, and neither ate nor drank.

Now there was a certain disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias!” He said, “Behold, it’s me, Lord.” The Lord said to him, “Arise, and go to the street which is called Straight, and inquire in the house of Judah for one named Saul, a man of Tarsus. For behold, he is praying, and in a vision he has seen a man named Ananias coming in, and laying his hands on him, that he might receive his sight.”
When the blood of Stephen, your witness, was shed, I also was standing by, and consenting to his death, and guarding the cloaks of those who killed him.’
But Ananias answered, “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he did to your saints at Jerusalem. Here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.”
He is asking you.
Write it down before the wind takes it.
Remember Isaiah’s promise to the eunuch who holds fast to the covenant.
He waves until the carriage is out of sight, singing something in a language you do not know. You are alone on the road with the wind.

lines.speaker: The official
lines.text: You are a scribe from Jerusalem. They turned me away from the inner courts. Tell me honestly: what is keeping me?
Philip woke you before dawn. He said an angel had spoken to him, and that you were to go south. You saw no angel. You went anyway.
“Nothing.”
Think of the Law that keeps men like him from the assembly, and say nothing.

lines.speaker: The official
lines.text: You are a woman of Jerusalem, and you can read. They turned me away from the inner courts. Tell me honestly: what is keeping me?
The Ethiopian official was baptized, Philip was caught away, and he went on his way rejoicing (Acts 8:38–39).
Two days later you find Philip in Azotus, preaching in the market as if nothing had happened. He says news has come from Jerusalem: Saul has letters from the high priest, and he is going to Damascus.
As it passes, you hear the man inside reading aloud in Greek, slowly, the way people read words they do not understand.
You tell him what Isaiah promised: that God will give eunuchs who keep his covenant a place in his house, and a name better than sons and daughters. His eyes fill.

Now the passage of the Scripture which he was reading was this, “He was led as a sheep to the slaughter. As a lamb before his shearer is silent, so he doesn’t open his mouth. In his humiliation, his judgment was taken away. Who will declare His generation? For his life is taken from the earth.”
The Spirit said to Philip, “Go near, and join yourself to this chariot.”
When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord caught Philip away, and the eunuch didn’t see him any more, for he went on his way rejoicing.

He arose and went; and behold, there was a man of Ethiopia, a eunuch of great authority under Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was over all her treasure, who had come to Jerusalem to worship. He was returning and sitting in his chariot, and was reading the prophet Isaiah.
But an angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying, “Arise, and go toward the south to the way that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza. This is a desert.”
As they went on the way, they came to some water, and the eunuch said, “Behold, here is water. What is keeping me from being baptized?”
He commanded the chariot to stand still, and they both went down into the water, both Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him.
But Philip was found at Azotus. Passing through, he preached the Good News to all the cities, until he came to Caesarea.
The eunuch answered Philip, “Who is the prophet talking about? About himself, or about someone else?” Philip opened his mouth, and beginning from this Scripture, preached to him Jesus.

Keep it on and watch.

Many spread their garments on the way, and others were cutting down branches from the trees, and spreading them on the road.

This was your uncle’s city, and yours. The place where you learned to pray is gone.

Say the Shema over the ruins.
